I do agree that we should support request headers, meta tags and similar 
for specifying the charset, not just a response header. And Elar is very 
correct in that UTF-7 makes XSS much (much) easier and is to be avoided.

- Jim

On 3/12/21 5:34 AM, Sjoerd Langkemper wrote:
>
>     Verify that every HTTP response contains a Content-Type header.
>     text/*, ///+xml and application/xml content types should also
>     specify a safe character set (e.g., UTF-8, ISO-8859-1).
>
> This implies that the charset should be set in the |Content-Type| 
> header, but I think it's also acceptable to set it in the content 
> itself, using |<meta charset="utf-8"/>| or |<?xml version="1.0" 
> encoding="UTF-8"?>|.
>
> For some content types such as text/plain, there is no security risk 
> when the charset is not defined. It could display certain characters 
> incorrectly, but that is not a security issue.
>
>     specify a safe character set
>
> Which character sets are "safe"? Aren't they all safe?
>
>     Verify that every HTTP non-static response contains a Content-Type
>     header.
>
> I am less sure about this distinction between static and dynamic 
> responses. What's dynamic can change over time, and even static files 
> are uploaded by someone. I think it's often hard to distinguish 
> between static and dynamic in practice.
>

This ASVS requirement has bothered me since version 3 (requirement 11.2). "What exactly is a safe character set?" is indeed the big question here. I tried to find out where this requirement came from, and discovered that [this bug in Apache](http://httpd.apache.org/info/css-security/apache_specific.html) has something to do with it: certain modules did not encode their output properly (according to the character set) and did not set an explicit character set. Many browsers back then autodetected UTF-7, and that made XSS possible.

IMO, the problem is not the character set, it is the mismatch between the character set assumed by one system (output encoding in the web application) and another (the browser). A character set being safe or unsafe depends entirely on how other systems handle it. In theory, if you specify your character set explicitly in a response, there should not be any problem, right? Only if other systems such as a browser ignore the character set, choose an alternative character set, or handle it insecurely, may there be a problem. I am not aware of any character sets being widely mishandled in browsers at the moment (except UTF-7 in (very) old browsers), but if there are, those would be the character sets to avoid.

Regarding header and `<meta http-equiv>`: response headers seem to have priority, but i could not find an authoritative reference for that. The HTML Living standard [says](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/semantics.html#character-encoding-declaration):

```
If an HTML document does not start with a BOM, and its encoding is not explicitly
given by Content-Type metadata, and the document is not an iframe srcdoc document,
then the encoding must be specified using a meta element with a charset attribute or a
meta element with an http-equiv attribute in the Encoding declaration state.
```

I am missing the 'only if' part, but my guess would be that browser would ignore the in-document character set specification if `Content-Type` specifies the character set.

14.4.1 could use some clarification. I suggest: 

```
Verify that every HTTP response contains a Content-Type header. text/*, */*+xml
and application/xml content types should also specify a "safe" character set, i.e.
one that browsers and other processors of the response implement and will
recognize correctly. UTF-8 and ISO-8859-1 are good choices.
```

This respects the fact that (other) character sets are not inherently insecure, and explains the cause of the problem, so that the reader can make a better decision. At the same time, it gives some suggestions that will likely be safe.

Headers are more secure than meta tags, as meta tags could be injected by an attacker. Meta tags were intended for situations where people could not control response headers. How likely would that be for a webapp developer? I think we can ignore meta tags in this requirement.


Tim
